---
title: "Comparing tests and training load"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 110, out.width = "100%")
library(lactater)
plex <- requireNamespace("systemfonts", quietly = TRUE) &&
  isTRUE(suppressMessages(systemfonts::require_font("IBM Plex Sans", fallback = "sans")))
if (plex) options(lactater.font = "IBM Plex Sans")
```

A step test is most useful the second time: did the athlete improve, by how much, and is that more than the noise
of the test? And between tests, how was the training spread across the zones? This article uses the six tests of
one trained cyclist in `lactate_tests` (real data from Trinity College Dublin, CC BY 4.0).

```{r}
series <- subset(lactate_tests, athlete == "cyclist_series")
unique(series[c("test", "day")])

analyse <- function(d) lactate_threshold(subset(series, day == d), intensity, lactate, heart_rate, plot = FALSE)
before <- analyse(0)
after <- analyse(58)
```

## Is the change real?

A threshold moves between two tests even when fitness does not, through day-to-day variation and the error of the
analyser and the method. `compare_tests()` gives every change an interval from the test-retest variation of the
method (Hopkins, 2000; Swinton et al., 2018) and calls it an increase or a decrease only when the whole interval is
on one side of zero, or of the smallest worthwhile change you set with `swc`.

```{r}
comparison <- compare_tests(before, after)
comparison[c("method", "before", "after", "change", "change_low", "change_high", "verdict")]
```

The default test-retest variation comes from trained male cyclists (Heuberger et al., 2018; Pallares et al., 2016)
and exists only for some methods; the others get a verdict once you give their `cv`, best measured on your own
athletes with your own protocol. `attr(comparison, "notes")` lists what could make two tests hard to compare: a
different protocol, sample type or resting sample, or a fall in peak lactate, which also moves the curve to the
right.

## How far did the curve move?

Thresholds are single points; the whole curve tells more. `curve_shift()` gives the intensity gained at each lactate,
and the lactate saved at the intensities you choose.

```{r}
curve_shift(before, after, intensity = c(250, 300))
autoplot(comparison)
```

## A series of tests

Over three or more tests, a straight-line trend with its interval shows the direction without reading noise from
one test to the next (Hopkins, 2017).

```{r, fig.height = 5.5}
days <- unique(series$day)
tests <- lapply(days, analyse)
trend <- do.call(lactate_trend, c(tests, list(day = days)))
trend[trend$method %in% c("OBLA 4.0", "ModDmax", "LTP2", "IAT"), ]
autoplot(trend, method = c("OBLA 4.0", "ModDmax", "LTP2", "IAT"))
```

## Comparing athletes

Per kg of body mass, and as a percentage of the highest intensity and heart rate of the test:

```{r}
relative <- relative_thresholds(after, body_mass = series$body_mass[series$day == 58][1])
columns <- c("method", "intensity", "intensity_per_kg", "percent_peak", "percent_peak_heart_rate")
relative[relative$method %in% c("Log-log", "ModDmax", "IAT"), columns]
```

A fixed lactate concentration falls at a similar percentage of peak power in trained and untrained people (Maassen &
Busse, 1989), so a percentage of peak does not rank fitness on its own.

## Training load in the zones

`training_load()` sorts the samples of training sessions into the zones of `lactate_zones()`: the time in each zone,
the training intensity distribution with its polarization index (Treff et al., 2019), and Lucia's training impulse.
Here, a made-up week of heart-rate data (one sample every 5 s) for this cyclist:

```{r}
zones <- lactate_zones(after, lt1 = "Log-log", lt2 = "ModDmax")
zones[c("zone", "heart_rate_from", "heart_rate_to")]

set.seed(1)
session <- function(name, minutes, heart_rate) {
  data.frame(session = name, heart_rate = round(stats::rnorm(minutes * 12, heart_rate, 3)))
}
week <- rbind(
  session("Mon easy", 90, 135),
  session("Tue intervals", 20, 140), session("Tue intervals", 24, 182), session("Tue intervals", 20, 140),
  session("Thu easy", 60, 138),
  session("Sat long", 240, 142),
  session("Sun tempo", 50, 165)
)
training_load(week, zones, interval = 5, .by = "session")
training_load(week, zones, interval = 5)
```

Heart rate lags behind intensity in short intervals, so heart-rate time in zone under-counts zone 3 in interval
sessions; power or speed samples (`measure = "intensity"`) avoid that (Seiler, 2010).
